analysis.one_liner: Quadruples the excise tax on corporate stock buybacks, from 1% to 4%.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company buys back its own stock, it pushes the share price up, which mainly rewards large shareholders and executives whose pay is tied to stock. Since 2023, such buybacks carry a 1% federal excise tax. This bill would have raised that tax to 4%, meaning companies that choose to hand cash back to shareholders instead of investing it or raising pay would pay more to the Treasury. It also would have exempted stock issued to certain employees from the tax's calculation rules.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public, indirectly: the extra tax revenue would flow to the Treasury like any federal revenue, available for regular government spending. To the extent the higher tax nudges companies toward wages, investment, or dividends instead of buybacks, ordinary workers and small retirement investors benefit modestly. No revenue in the bill is earmarked for a specific program.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the excise tax on corporate stock repurchases from 1% to 4%, tripling the cost to companies of buying back their own shares.
Exempts the value of stock issued to covered employees from the tax's adjustment rules, so firms are not penalized for shares given to workers under the definitions in section 162(m).
Applies to repurchases occurring after enactment, so it takes effect immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations and their shareholders, especially the largest ones, would pay more whenever they repurchase stock. Executives and wealthy households hold most shares, so the cost would fall mostly on them, with some spillover to any investor whose funds trade around buyback announcements.

drawbacks.text: Buybacks are not inherently harmful: they return cash to shareholders, including pension funds and retirement savers, and a higher tax could lead some companies to borrow instead, since debt payments are deductible while the buyback tax is not.

The bill raises revenue for the general fund without directing it to any specific purpose, so its practical benefit to ordinary people depends entirely on how Congress later chooses to spend the money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A reasonable but modest policy: it makes a corporate practice slightly more expensive and raises revenue, without banning anything. The main weakness is that the benefit to ordinary people is diffuse and unspecified, while the cost is concentrated and visible to corporate treasurers. It would not by itself change how most companies deploy capital.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sherrod Brown introduced the bill in the Senate on February 14, 2023, with six original cosponsors including Ron Wyden, the Finance Committee chair.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; that referral was its final action.
The bill attracted nine cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support.
No committee markup, hearing, floor vote, or House companion action appears in the record; the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and large shareholders are better off, because the buyback tax stays at 1% rather than rising to 4%.

against.what_they_did: No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan base typically needed to reach the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All nine cosponsors were Democrats, including the Finance Committee chair, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: They would have paid 4% instead of 1% on every share repurchase, making the shareholder-cash-return strategy more expensive. For the public, that means more corporate cash flowing to the Treasury or, in theory, toward wages and investment.

industries.industry: Large shareholders, executives, and asset managers
industries.note: Buybacks lift share prices, and these groups hold most shares and much executive pay is stock-based. A 4% tax trims the after-tax value of that channel, while ordinary retirement savers would feel it only slightly and indirectly.
